questionText:
Suppose you are asked to design a new reliable byte-stream transport protocol like TCP. This protocol, named $\texttt{myTCP}$, runs over a 100 Mbps network with Round Trip Time of 150 milliseconds and the maximum segment lifetime of 2 minutes.

Which of the following is/are valid lengths of the Sequence Number field in the $\texttt{myTCP}$ header?
explanation:
To prevent sequence number wrap-around during the Maximum Segment Lifetime (MSL), the total number of unique sequence numbers must be large enough so that sequence numbers are not reused within the MSL duration.

Given:
Bandwidth = $100\text{ Mbps} = \frac{100 \times 10^6}{8}\text{ bytes/sec} = 12.5 \times 10^6\text{ bytes/sec}$
Maximum Segment Lifetime (MSL) = $2\text{ minutes} = 120\text{ seconds}$

Step 1: Calculate the maximum bytes transmitted during MSL:
$\text{Max Bytes Transmitted} = \text{Bandwidth} \times \text{MSL}$
$\text{Max Bytes Transmitted} = 12.5 \times 10^6\text{ bytes/sec} \times 120\text{ sec} = 1.5 \times 10^9\text{ bytes}$

Step 2: Determine the minimum number of bits ($N$) required:
$2^N \ge 1.5 \times 10^9$

Checking powers of 2:
$2^{30} = 1,073,741,824 \text{ bytes} < 1.5 \times 10^9\text{ bytes}$ (30 bits is NOT enough)
$2^{31} = 2,147,483,648 \text{ bytes} > 1.5 \times 10^9\text{ bytes}$ (Minimum required is 31 bits)

Conclusion:
Any field length greater than or equal to $31\text{ bits}$ is valid. Thus, $32\text{ bits}$, $34\text{ bits}$, and $36\text{ bits}$ are all valid sequence number field lengths.
